identity.name: Ashwagandha
identity.name_meaning: Aśvagandhā is traditionally explained in relation to the horse-like odour of the root and the strength associated with a horse.

classification.habitat: Subtropical, semi-arid and relatively dry regions
classification.distribution: Native range extends from southern Europe to Central China and from Africa to Myanmar; present in India and many other regions.

identification.description: An erect, branched, tomentose subshrub with ovate leaves, small greenish-yellow flowers and globose red berries enclosed by an enlarged persistent calyx.
identification.whole_plant: Small erect branched shrub or subshrub, commonly about 0.5–2 m depending on growing conditions, with greyish or whitish tomentose stems.
identification.root: The medicinal part in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia is the dried mature root. Roots are generally stout, tapering and branched, with a characteristic odour.
identification.stem: Erect, branched and greyish-tomentose; young stems are covered with fine hairs.
identification.leaf: Simple, generally ovate to obovate or oblong, with entire or nearly entire margins; leaves may be tomentose, especially beneath.
identification.flower: Small, greenish to yellowish flowers occurring mainly in axillary clusters.
identification.fruit: Globose berry, approximately 5–8 mm in diameter, shiny and red when mature, enclosed by and exceeded by the enlarged persistent calyx.
identification.seed: Small, approximately 2 mm in diameter, reticulate seeds.
identification.bark: Stem bark is not the official Ayurvedic drug part. The official medicinal material is the dried mature root.
identification_points: Enlarged persistent calyx surrounding the fruit
Dried mature root is the official Ayurvedic drug material

dravya_guna.source_note: Ayurvedic property descriptions vary somewhat among secondary databases and publications. The values above follow the pharmacological profile reported in Ayurvedic sources consulted during this research; the primary edition/page should be checked before marking a classical citation as fully verified.

dosha.pitta: May increase with excessive use because of Ushna Virya
dosha.kapha: Generally described as Kapha-modulating; classical descriptions vary by source
dosha.overall: Primarily used as a Vata-pacifying and strengthening drug; exact Dosha interpretation should be read with Rasa, Guna and Virya.

therapeutics.dose: Root powder: 3–6 g/day according to CCRAS technical specifications citing the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India.
therapeutics.anupana: Anupana is preparation- and indication-dependent; milk and ghee are traditionally used with suitable Ashwagandha preparations, but the vehicle should not be treated as universal.
therapeutics.duration: Condition-dependent; duration should be determined according to formulation, indication and professional clinical assessment.
precautions: Do not automatically substitute leaf preparations for the official root drug.
Dose of a standardized extract cannot be directly equated with the dose of crude root powder.
Use cautiously when there may be drug interactions or relevant medical conditions.
contraindications: Breastfeeding: NCCIH advises avoiding use because safety information is insufficient.
Autoimmune disorders: NCCIH advises against use.
Thyroid disorders: NCCIH advises against use.
therapeutics.modern_safety_note: NCCIH reports that short-term use up to about 3 months may be safe for some people, but long-term safety is not established. Reported adverse effects include drowsiness, gastrointestinal upset, diarrhoea and vomiting; rare cases of liver injury have also been reported.

phytochemistry.chemical_notes: Withania somnifera contains steroidal lactones called withanolides, along with alkaloids, glycosides, sitoindosides and other constituents. Chemical composition varies according to plant part, geography, genotype and extraction method.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Modern clinical evidence is preparation-specific and varies by condition. NCCIH reports that some ashwagandha preparations may help with insomnia and stress, while evidence for several other proposed uses remains insufficient or unclear. Many studies are small and use different preparations.
research_findings: Some clinical trials suggest benefit for stress-related outcomes.
Some studies suggest improvement in sleep in selected populations.
Limited evidence suggests possible increases in testosterone and sperm quality after 2–4 months in some men.
Evidence is insufficient for many other promoted indications.
modern_information.safety_notes: Rare liver injury has been reported. Possible adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, diarrhoea, vomiting and drowsiness. Potential interactions have been reported with medicines for diabetes, hypertension, immunosuppressants, sedatives, anticonvulsants and thyroid hormone medicines.
modern_information.regulatory_note: The Government of India's Ministry of AYUSH states that the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia defines Ashwagandha as the dried mature roots of Withania somnifera Dunal and has advised against use of its leaves as an ASU medicinal ingredient because their use has not been reported in the classical ASU texts.

student.quick_revision: Ashwagandha = Withania somnifera, Solanaceae, dried mature root, Madhura-Tikta-Kashaya, Laghu-Snigdha, Ushna, Madhura Vipaka, Rasayana-Balya-Vajikarana.

teaching_points: Demonstrate the difference between botanical plant morphology and the official medicinal part.
Show the enlarged persistent calyx around the berry as an important identification character.
Explain the relationship between Rasa, Guna and Virya when discussing Dosha action.
Discuss why root authentication and correct plant identification are important in crude-drug quality control.
Compare classical root use with modern research on root extracts.
discussion_points: Classical identity and synonyms of Ashwagandha
Official pharmacopoeial part versus other plant parts
practical_points: Record botanical name and family correctly

doctor.quick_reference: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an Ayurvedic Rasayana and Balya drug for which the official Ayurvedic medicinal material is the dried mature root.
doctor.dose: Root powder 3–6 g/day; formulation-specific dosing differs.
doctor.anupana: Depends on indication and formulation; traditionally milk or ghee may be used in appropriate preparations.
key_precautions: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding according to NCCIH.
Avoid before surgery according to NCCIH.
Use caution in autoimmune and thyroid disorders.
Monitor for gastrointestinal adverse effects and rare liver injury.
Do not equate concentrated extract doses with crude root-powder doses.
doctor.evidence_note: Modern evidence is preparation-specific. Some evidence supports possible benefits for stress and insomnia, while evidence for many other promoted uses remains insufficient.
